title: Meningioma of Foramen Magnum Causing Drop Attacks
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old woman with hypertension presented with sudden episodes of falling to the ground without loss of consciousness over the past 5 months. Each episode lasted approximately 1 minute and was followed by full neurological recovery. She experienced 1–2 such events per day, often associated with giddiness. On examination, she had mild hyperreflexia in all four limbs but no other focal deficits.

Diagnostic studies included:
• Twenty-four-hour electroencephalography, which was normal.  
• Electromyography and nerve conduction studies of all four limbs, which were normal.  
• Cardiovascular evaluation, including electrocardiography and Holter monitoring, which were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Epilepsy was considered but excluded — “Twenty-four-hour electroencephalography (EEG) … was normal.”  
2. Neuromuscular disorders were considered but excluded — “Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction velocity (NCV) of all four limbs were also normal.”  
3. Cardiac arrhythmias were considered but excluded — “Cardiovascular workup which included echocardiograms (ECG) and Holter monitoring were normal.”  
4. Cataplexy, psychogenic “syncope,” and transient ischaemic attacks were part of the differential for falls without loss of consciousness — “Falls without loss of consciousness can be due to cataplexy, drop attacks, psychogenic ‘syncope’ … and transient ischaemic attacks.”  
5. Vestibular disorders such as Ménière disease and migrainous vertigo can cause drop attacks — “The causes of drop attacks include … inner ear disorders (e.g., Ménière disease and migrainous vertigo) …”  
6. Cervical cord compression and vertebrobasilar ischemia are recognized etiologies of drop attacks — “The causes of drop attacks include cervical cord compression, vertebrobasilar ischemia …”  
7. Hydrocephalus and myxedema may present with sudden falls — “The causes of drop attacks include … hydrocephalus, and myxedema.”  
8. Intracranial and craniospinal tumors can cause drop attacks, most often via hydrocephalus; imaging was thus pursued — “We found four cases of craniospinal tumors causing drop attacks …”  
9. MRI demonstrated a dural‐based, homogenously enhancing lesion encasing the left vertebral artery in the foramen magnum, indicating the final diagnosis — “Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed anterolaterally placed, homogenously enhancing dural based lesion in the foramen magnum encasing the left vertebral artery suggestive of meningioma …”
